evidence_quotes.quote: China’s South–North Water Transfer Project (SNWTP), known in Chinese as Nanshui beidiao, is one of the world’s largest construction projects. If fully completed, the SNWTP will eventually transfer some 45 billion cubic metres of water annually from southern to northern China, transforming the country’s environmental, economic, and political geography.
In the remainder of this discussion, I attempt to explain both the persistence of the SNWTP as a technocratic, authoritarian response to water scarcity and the absence of social mobilisation.

My account stresses how, even in a contested, pluralising, and modernised political environment, an authoritarian government can mount large-scale, technocratic, and top-down solutions to environmental policy problems.

Primary data collection consisted of 43 key-informant interviews and Chinese-language source collection in three Chinese cities. The sample includes 15 academics, 8 activists or NGO representatives, 5 journalists, 6 independent researchers, and 9 active or former government officials.

However, the SNWTP example adds a twist to the AE literature by illustrating how authoritarian governments apply a mixture of persuasion and coercion to co-opt as well as stymie opposition to its objectives.

criterion_notes.c1: No. The paper is a macro-political environmental governance study of China's South-North Water Transfer Project (SNWTP), an inter-basin bulk water-resource transfer mega-project. Consistent with Exclusion Criterion 7 (water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access), it examines pollution along transfer canals, displacement/resettlement of reservoir migrants, and central-local provincial bargaining, rather than household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: No under the active 2026-10-13 rule-type reading; Yes under the plain broad wording. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper examines governance, administrative, and institutional factors (authoritarian environmental policymaking, central-local intergovernmental compensation, state-owned project governance, and migrant resettlement regulations). However, under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, it fails Criterion 2 because it analyses macro-political persuasive messaging, co-optation of provincial opposition, and generic mega-project governance rather than any rule-type mechanism (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, administrative burden, or utility regulatory structure) directly governing household or community water/sanitation service access. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because C1 and C4 are not met.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. The author conducts an empirical qualitative descriptive case study drawing on 43 primary key-informant interviews in three Chinese cities (15 academics, 8 activists/NGO representatives, 5 journalists, 6 independent researchers, and 9 current/former government officials) alongside Chinese-language documentary sources.
criterion_notes.c4: No. Reported outcomes concern muted civil society mobilisation, containment of sub-national provincial opposition via fiscal/infrastructure side-payments, ecological disruption and canal pollution control investments, and social dislocation/stipends among displaced reservoir residents. No outcomes measuring household or community water or sanitation access, connection, service continuity, reliability, quantity, affordability, or service exclusion are reported.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Within its environmental politics research scope, the study design (qualitative descriptive case study), unit of analysis and sample (the SNWTP national mega-project and 43 key informants), political governance exposures, and political/environmental/resettlement outcomes are clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is published in English.

study_design: Qualitative descriptive case study using 43 key-informant interviews and Chinese-language documentary analysis
population_and_sample: Case study of China's South-North Water Transfer Project (national/inter-provincial political arena); primary interview sample of 43 key informants in three Chinese cities (15 academics, 8 activists or NGO representatives, 5 journalists, 6 independent researchers, and 9 active or former government officials)
exposure: Authoritarian environmental governance strategies by China's central government (persuasive public messaging, canal pollution-control investments, reservoir migrant resettlement policies, and intergovernmental compensation/side-payments to water-exporting provinces)
outcome: Political contestation and muted civil society mobilisation around the SNWTP, containment of provincial opposition, ecological disruption along transfer routes, and displacement/resettlement impacts (no household or community water or sanitation service access outcomes reported)
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic): this qualitative case study tests Ecological Modernisation and Authoritarian Environmentalism theories against the macro-politics of China's inter-basin South-North Water Transfer Project (pollution control, reservoir resettlement, and central-local intergovernmental bargaining). Per Exclusion Criterion 7, it is a water-resource/infrastructure politics study unrelated to household or community water or sanitation service access (failing C1), examines no rule-type mechanism governing service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification (failing narrow C2), and reports no household or community service access outcomes (failing C4). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, it remains excluded due to failing C1 and C4.
